themes: Clinical progression to MCI and dementia
one_line: Cognitively unimpaired individuals with both amyloid and tau PET positivity—especially those with tau pathology in the neocortex—are at significantly higher risk for short-term clinical progression to MCI and all-cause dementia than biomarker-negative individuals.
summary: This large multicenter longitudinal study evaluated 1,325 cognitively unimpaired individuals to determine if the combined presence of amyloid-β and tau pathology (measured via PET) predicts short-term cognitive decline. Participants were classified into biomarker profile groups: A-T-, A+T-, A+T MTL+ (tau in the medial temporal lobe only), and A+T NEO-T+ (tau in the temporal neocortex). Over an average follow-up of 41.8 months, the A+T NEO-T+ and A+T MTL+ groups showed a substantially increased risk of progressing to mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and all-cause dementia compared to the A-T- reference group. Furthermore, tau-positive groups exhibited significantly faster longitudinal global cognitive decline than both A-T- and A+T- individuals. The findings support the NIA-AA criteria defining A+T+ individuals as having 'preclinical Alzheimer's disease', emphasizing that combined amyloid and tau positivity indicates advanced pathological changes and a highly elevated risk of short-term clinical progression rather than merely being a risk factor.

key_claims.claim: Cognitively unimpaired individuals with amyloid and tau PET positivity have a substantially increased risk of progressing to MCI.
key_claims.evidence: Cox proportional-hazards models showed a hazard ratio of 19.2 (95% CI 10.9–33.7) for the A+T NEO-T+ group and 14.6 (95% CI 8.1–26.4) for the A+T MTL+ group compared to the A-T- group.

key_claims.claim: Tau positivity in the neocortex carries an exceptionally high risk for short-term progression to all-cause dementia.
key_claims.evidence: Cox proportional-hazards models showed a hazard ratio of 41.3 (95% CI 16.7–101.9, P < 0.001) for progression to all-cause dementia in the A+T NEO-T+ group versus the A-T- group.
key_claims.location: Results (Clinical progression to all-cause dementia) / Fig 2

key_claims.claim: Individuals with both amyloid and tau pathology decline cognitively faster than those with amyloid pathology alone.
key_claims.evidence: Linear mixed-effect models for the mPACC5 composite score indicated that A+T NEO-T+ and A+T MTL+ groups progressed significantly faster than the A+T- group.

methods.population: Cognitively unimpaired individuals from 7 cohorts (MCSA, BioFINDER-1, BioFINDER-2, BACS, HABS, AIBL, ADC)

limitations: Inherent challenges due to the multicenter study design, including data pooling, harmonization, different amyloid and tau PET tracers, and dissimilarities in PET acquisition protocols.
Different neuropsychological tests were used as mPACC5 subcomponents across cohorts.
Relatively low number of clinical events, particularly for progression to dementia.
Potential consent/volunteer bias (lower study participation among individuals at risk) and informative censoring (drop out when experiencing symptoms).
Study design only allowed establishing relative risk rather than lifetime risk, and did not control for the competing risk of death in survival analyses.
red_flags: The A-T+ group was excluded from the main analyses (relegated to extended data) because it was 'considerably smaller' (n=34). While justified by statistical power, excluding isolated tau positivity prevents a full factorial evaluation of tau's impact independent of amyloid.
